new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive but confined to a two-syllable initial window: every word carries its one contrastive (emic) stress on either the first or the second syllable (minimal pairs 'ata 'bone' vs a'ta 'ear', 'uhijo 'smell' vs u'hijo 'roll', 'samakavo 'I find' vs a'manavo 'I fasten'); further stresses fall rhythmically on every alternate syllable after the contrastive one and are non-contrastive. Per the orthography note (ms p.35) the less frequent patterns are second-syllable stress in disyllables and initial stress in three- and four-syllable words, i.e. disyllables are usually initial-stressed and longer words usually second-syllable-stressed. The 1992 OPD restates: 'Stress is phonemic.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Non-contrastive rhythmic stress on every alternate syllable after the contrastive stress (5.3.1); in '_ _ _ _ words the predictable third-syllable stress is often heavier than the contrastive first-syllable stress, intensities fluctuate (5.3.2.3, ms p.26); /i'u/ and /u'V/ count as two syllables for stress placement (5.3.3.1-2).
new_statements.exceptions: A few grammatical words consist of two phonological words with two emic stresses, e.g. /'tati?i'ura/ 'bug', /si'u?usi'u?u/ 'early morning' (5.3.3.3, ms p.29); greater tendency for first-syllable stress in four-syllable 'CVV CVV words (5.3.2.3).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word, citation forms from a c.700-word corpus (Numba village speakers). 5.3.4: the emic stress of the phrase-final word is stronger, higher pitched and lengthened, with a general upglide at the end of every pause group in narrative.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Parlier sources describe Managalasi (= Ese, mcq, esee1247) as spoken at Numba village near the Sila airstrip (central Managalasi); Dutton 1969 lists up to eleven Managalasi 'isolects', so the statement is for the Numba variety. SIL PNG catalogues the language as 'Ese [mcq]'.

new_statements.quote: The Managalasi phonemes are a (ə unstressed following vowels, a elsewhere), ch (voiceless alveopalatal affricate), e (ɛ word finally, e elsewhere), h, i, j (voiced alveo-palatal affricate), k, m, n, o (ɔ word finally following bilabials, o elsewhere), p, r (retroflexed flap, and fluctuating with a lateral flap before u and i), s, t, u, ú (high central rounded ʉ), v (voiced bilabial fricative), ' (glottal stop), and ´ (stress, marked only on the second syllable of two-syllable words, and on a stressed vowel preceded by a non-syllabic u.

new_statements.rule_in_words: A morphology paper; its only stress statement is an orthographic convention in a footnote: the stress mark is written only on the second syllable of two-syllable words (and on a stressed vowel after non-syllabic u). This presupposes that disyllables contrast initial (unmarked, default) and second-syllable (marked) stress; nothing is said about longer words.

new_statements.identity_note: All six works are by the Parliers (SIL) on the Numba-village variety: the 1963 phonology data come from two young men from Numba near the Sila airstrip (ms p.1), the 1970 and 1973 papers state 'the materials for this paper were gathered in the village of Numba', and the 1981 dictionary preface (p.iv) notes 'dialectical differences among the 5,000 speakers of which Numba Village, whose dialect this book is based upon, is considered to be the central point of the language'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Only the first stress in a word is contrastive, and it falls on either the first or the second syllable (minimal pairs for 2-, 3- and 4-syllable words, e.g. 'ata 'bone' vs a'ta 'ear', 'uhijo 'smell' vs u'hijo 'roll', 'kasima 'boy' vs ka'tija 'basket'). Which of the two a word takes is lexical. Later stresses are rhythmic, every other syllable after the contrastive one.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Stress tends to occur every alternate syllable following the contrastive stress' (5.3.1); in four-syllable words of the '__ __ __ __ pattern the predictable third-syllable stress is often heavier than the contrastive first-syllable stress (5.3.2.3); secondary stress is shown phonetically in /i'u/ and /u'V/ sequences, which count as two syllables for stress (5.3.3.1-2).
new_statements.exceptions: 5.3.3.3: 'A few grammatical words consist of two phonological words with two emic stresses' (e.g. glosses 'bug', 'early morning', 'stone axe', 'stomach'). Orthography note ms p.35: 'In symbolizing stress we would like: __'__; '__ __ __; and '__ __ __ __. These patterns occur less frequently and therefore can best be handled in this way' - i.e. second-syllable stress is the minority pattern in disyllables, but initial stress is the minority pattern in three- and four-syllable words.
new_statements.identity_note: All six works are by the Parliers (SIL) on the Numba-village variety: the 1963 phonology data come from two young men from Numba near the Sila airstrip (ms p.1), the 1970 and 1973 papers state 'the materials for this paper were gathered in the village of Numba', and the 1981 dictionary preface (p.iv) notes 'dialectical differences among the 5,000 speakers of which Numba Village, whose dialect this book is based upon, is considered to be the central point of the language'.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on the phonology: every Parlier source that speaks to it says stress is contrastive between the first and second syllable of the word (1963 phonology, 1992 OPD), and the 1970 sentences, 1973 verbs and 1981 dictionary presuppose the same contrast through their orthographic marking. The only differences are orthographic: the 1963 phonology proposed writing the less frequent patterns (second-syllable stress in disyllables, initial stress in three- and four-syllable words); the 1970/1973 papers and the 1992 OPD write only second-syllable stress in disyllables (plus stressed vowels after non-syllabic u); the 1981 dictionary writes the 1963 pair /ata/ 'bone' vs /a'ta/ 'ear' as 'ata vs ataa while using an acute elsewhere (aakuá, apúsavo). Dutton 1969 (already held by the project, second-hand) reports the same contrast on first and second syllables.

sources.note: Second-hand. Sec. 5.83.73 (p.145-146): 'J. and J. Parlier show stress to be contrastive on first and second syllables of words.' Sec. 5.82: 'In the three languages of the Family studied in more detail (viz., Koiari, Aomie, and Managalasi) stress has been found to be phonemic.' Also notes Parliers treat [ʉ] as /iu/ with stress on the second vowel.

sources.note: Sec. 5.3.1 (ms p.24-25): only the first stress in a word is contrastive; stress then falls on every alternate syllable after it. Sec. 5.3.2 (ms pp.25-27): emic stress patterns for 2-, 3- and 4-syllable words are initial vs. second-syllable stress ('ata 'bone' / a'ta 'ear'; 'uhijo 'smell' / u'hijo 'roll'; 'samakavo 'I find' / a'manavo 'I fasten'); in '_ _ _ _ the predictable third-syllable stress is often heavier than the contrastive first. 5.3.3.3: a few grammatical words are two phonological words with two emic stresses.
